narrative:
The model determined that you have a 72% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three pieces of information about you drove that decision, ranked from most to least influential. First, your undergraduate GPA of 2.60 stood out as the strongest factor. While the typical student who is accepted has a GPA of 3.23, yours is noticeably lower. This pulled the prediction strongly toward failure.

Second, your family income bracket of upper-middle class also worked against you. Although this is the most common background among accepted students, in your specific combination of circumstances the model interpreted it as increasing the likelihood of struggling with the bar exam.

Third, your first-year law school grades placed you in the 7th decile. This was actually better than the average of accepted students, so it pushed the prediction slightly toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to outweigh the concerns raised by your GPA and family income.

The combination of these factors led the system to conclude your risk of failing the bar was too high for admission. To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your academic performance, particularly by strengthening your study habits and seeking support to boost your grades. Consider reapplying once you have a clearer record of stronger performance. (218 words)
